implementation_notes: Combine ships the two halves directly: CurrentValueSubject wraps a single value and publishes a new element whenever the value changes - the current state plus a replay-one stream for new subscribers - while a PassthroughSubject carries events into the reducer; SwiftUI observes the component through @StateObject/ObservableObject with @Published properties or through .onReceive on the state publisher. The component is a final class (typically @MainActor) whose methods are the handlers, and cancellables must be stored or subscriptions end with the scope.
pitfalls: A subscription not held in an AnyCancellable is cancelled as soon as its scope ends - the classic 'nothing happens' Combine bug.
Publishing from a background thread while SwiftUI reads state breaks main-thread guarantees: annotate the component @MainActor and hop before mutating state.
CurrentValueSubject replays its value to every new subscriber, so one-shot effects (navigation, alerts) put into the state stream re-fire on re-subscription.

Retain cycles: closures capturing self strongly, or children holding the view model, keep the component and its state alive after the screen is gone - capture [weak self] or rely on @StateObject's lifetime.

variants.name: Observation framework (@Observable) with async sequences (iOS 17+)
variants.implementation_notes: Since iOS 17 and macOS 14 the Observation framework does what Combine publishers did by hand: the @Observable macro implements the Observable protocol at compile time, SwiftUI tracks exactly the properties a view reads (withObservationTracking records property access inside its apply closure), and the Observations type exposes an asynchronous sequence of tracked changes for non-SwiftUI consumers. Events stay plain methods on an @MainActor class and the state is a struct property, so the component collapses into an observable state machine object - the closest thing to the original pattern in Swift; use it for new code and keep Combine where its operators or older OS floors are required.
pitfalls: Observation tracks only properties that were read inside withObservationTracking's apply closure - a view that never reads a property is never notified when it changes.
The macro instruments stored properties at compile time: computed properties are not tracked unless they read tracked storage, and @ObservationIgnored silently removes a dependency.
AsyncStream continuations must be finished or the consumer leaks, and dropping a continuation stops updates for that subscriber without an error.
Accessing @Observable state from background tasks is still a data race; keep the component on the main actor, since SwiftUI's rendering assumes it.
